What are the new heaven and the new earth?
Answer
In Revelation 21:1, John sees something spectacular: “Then I saw ‘a new heaven and a new earth,’ for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.” This new earth and new heaven are sometimes referred to as the “eternal state.” As seen in Revelation chapters 21—22, the new earth will be the eternal dwelling place of believers in Jesus Christ. Scripture gives us a few details of the new heaven and new earth.

The current heaven and earth have long been subject to God’s curse because of mankind’s sin. All creation “has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth” (Romans 8:22) as it awaits the fulfillment of God’s plan and “the children of God to be revealed” (verse 19). Heaven and earth will pass away (Mark 13:31), and they will be replaced by the new heaven and the new earth. At that time, the Lord, seated on His throne, says, “I am making everything new!” (Revelation 21:5). In the new creation, sin will be totally eradicated, and “there shall be no more curse” (Revelation 22:3, NKJV).

The new heaven and new earth are also mentioned in Isaiah 65:17; 66:22; and 2 Peter 3:13. Peter says that the new heaven and new earth will be “where righteousness dwells.” Isaiah says that “the former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind.” Things will be completely new, and the old order of things, with the accompanying sorrow and tragedy, will be gone.

The new earth will be free from sin, evil, sickness, suffering, and death. It will be earth as God originally intended it to be, prior to the curse of sin. It will be Eden restored.

A major feature of the new earth will be the New Jerusalem. John calls it “the Holy City . . . coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband” (Revelation 21:2). This glorious city, with its streets of gold and pearly gates, is situated on a new, glorious earth. The tree of life will be there (Revelation 22:2). This city represents the final state of redeemed mankind, forever in fellowship with God: “God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. . . . His servants will serve him. They will see his face” (Revelation 21:3; 22:3–4).

In the new heaven and new earth, Scripture says, there are seven things notable for their absence—seven things that are “no more”:
• no more sea (Revelation 21:1)
• no more death (Revelation 21:4)
• no more mourning (Revelation 21:4)
• no more weeping (Revelation 21:4)
• no more pain (Revelation 21:4)
• no more curse (Revelation 22:3)
• no more night (Revelation 22:5)

The creation of the new heaven and new earth brings the promise that God “will wipe every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4). This event comes after the tribulation, after the Lord’s second coming, after the millennial kingdom, after the final rebellion, after the final judgment of Satan, and after the great white throne judgment. The brief description of the new heaven and new earth is the last glimpse into eternity that the Bible gives.

The Packers offer an important lesson.
Ownership does not have to mean:
“Whoever has the most money gets control.”
The Packers have been community-owned since 1923. Their supporters have repeatedly helped finance the organization, while the structure prevents one individual from taking control.
That is not socialism.
It is not capitalism in its usual corporate form.
It is something Wisconsin has understood remarkably well:
An institution can belong to the people who care about its future.
Perhaps we should study that idea beyond football.

text:
Summary from Grok-

Here are documented, named examples of farms and rural properties facing loss of land (or major operational disruption) specifically for high-voltage transmission lines built to serve data-center power demand. In most cases the utility seeks a permanent easement rather than buying the entire farm; the line still cuts through fields, restricts farming practices (irrigation, crop-dusting, electric fencing, livestock), lowers remaining land value, and sometimes requires removing buildings.

Grant County, Washington (Quincy data-center hub)  
Grant County PUD is condemning portions of farms and homes for a 31-mile 230 kV line from Wanapum Dam to Quincy. Data centers already use 37% of the county’s power. The line crosses 112 parcels, including agricultural land and 34 homes.  
Farmer Darrin Reynolds (corn and alfalfa): the line would block his electric fence for cattle and endanger crop-dusting pilots. His daughter canceled plans to build a house on the farm. Quote: “My land is being stolen for the benefit of these data centers.”  
Lisa Marcusen was offered $20,000 for a half-mile, 50-foot strip.  
A judge ruled in August 2026 that the PUD can take the land; landowners are appealing. Construction is slated to start in 2028.

Gaver Farm, Mount Airy, Maryland  
Lisa and Mike Gaver’s seventh-generation 150–165-acre Christmas-tree, pumpkin, and agritourism farm sits on the preferred route of the 67-mile, 500 kV Maryland Piedmont Reliability Project (often called an “extension cord” for Northern Virginia data centers). The line would cut diagonally through a 40-acre Christmas-tree field that holds roughly $4 million in inventory and would also take out hayride paths and woods. Lisa Gaver: “It’s going to financially devastate us.” Local officials and hundreds of residents have opposed it; eminent domain has been described as a last-resort option.

Clarke County, Virginia (252-year-old farm)  
A ninth-generation family farm (original Lord Fairfax deed, pre-dating the United States) on 37 acres is in the path of Dominion Energy’s proposed 765 kV North Valley Link line (more than 250 miles long). The company has said the project is needed in part to serve growing data-center load. The line would run through the farm’s drain field, front yard, and next to the house. The family wants it to become a 10th-generation farm. This is the case featured in the recent ABC 7 short you posted.

Coweta and Fayette Counties, Georgia (Project Wansley)  
Georgia Power’s 35-mile 500 kV line (part of a much larger grid expansion) is expected to serve data centers for 70–80% of its new capacity. It crosses more than 330 properties; 20–30 homes are slated for demolition.  
Ansley Brown’s childhood home is being taken; she has called it “theft.”  
Residents report compensation offers well below what they believe their properties are worth. Eminent domain is being used after negotiations fail.

Southeastern Wisconsin (Ozaukee County / Port Washington data-center campus)  
American Transmission Co.’s proposed high-voltage line for a large AI data-center campus would cut a 250-foot-wide path through private land, including a 70-acre property, the area’s largest dairy farm, an apple orchard, and organic farms. Landowners argue the line is driven by one private customer rather than general public need.

These are active or recently ruled cases with named landowners, specific utilities, and published reporting. The common thread is that the new lines are justified as grid reliability projects, yet utilities and grid operators have acknowledged that data-center growth is a primary driver of the added capacity. If you need links to the original articles or more detail on any one case, say which one.
